analysis.one_liner: Requires seat belts, anti-ejection windows, and fire and rollover safety equipment on new buses, plus stricter vetting of bus companies and drivers.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bus safety bill cleared the Senate Commerce Committee without recorded opposition, but the full Senate never voted on it before that Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Transportation Department to require seat belts at every seat, windows that stop passengers from being thrown out, stronger roofs, rollover-stability technology, tire pressure monitors, and better fire equipment on new motorcoaches. It would have forced safety audits of new bus companies before they can operate, safety ratings for all operators every three years, tougher training and testing for bus drivers, tamper-resistant electronic logs of driver hours, and new rules against companies dodging safety orders by operating under common ownership or family ties. The Senate Commerce Committee approved it favorably and placed it on the Senate calendar, but no floor vote ever happened.
analysis.who_benefits: Passengers on intercity and charter buses, who get crash protection and fire safety improvements, plus better-vetted companies and less-fatigued, better-trained drivers. Honest operators also gain a more level field against cut-rate carriers that cut safety corners.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Transportation Secretary to write rules requiring seat belts at every seating position, anti-ejection window glazing, stronger roofs, electronic stability control, tire pressure monitoring, and improved firefighting equipment on new motorcoaches.

Bars the Secretary from registering a new bus company until it passes an on-site pre-authorization safety audit covering drug and alcohol testing, driver qualifications, insurance, and maintenance programs, and requires a safety fitness rating for every operator, updated at least every three years.

Prohibits two or more bus operators from using common ownership, management, control, or family relationships to avoid or conceal noncompliance with commercial bus safety rules, letting the Secretary deny or revoke registration of such 'reincarnated' carriers.
Requires tamper-resistant electronic on-board recorders on interstate motorcoaches that accurately log driver hours of service, aimed at fatigued driving.

Requires minimum training curricula for entry-level bus drivers, including fire suppression and passenger evacuation skills, a stricter commercial driver's license passenger-endorsement exam, and a national registry of qualified medical examiners for commercial drivers.

analysis.who_pays: Bus manufacturers bear the cost of adding equipment to new buses; bus operators pay for electronic logs, driver training, and up to a $1,200 pre-authorization audit fee for new entrants. Some of these costs would show up in ticket prices.

drawbacks.text: Equipment mandates on new buses add manufacturing costs that would flow through to ticket prices for bus travelers.
The bill lets the Secretary charge new entrants a fee of up to $1,200 for the pre-authorization safety audit, a startup cost that weighs most heavily on small operators.
New training and endorsement requirements before a driver can take the passenger-endorsement test could shrink the pool of qualified drivers and raise hiring costs for small carriers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is straightforward: more crash and fire protection for bus passengers at the price of higher equipment, training, and compliance costs. The reported version softened the blow by applying most equipment mandates only to buses built more than two years after each final rule, with retrofits of older fleets left to a feasibility assessment, and the $1,200 audit fee covers the government's own cost of vetting new operators. The costs are real but modest compared with what rollover and fire crashes cost in lives, and the bill's harshest effects fall on the least safe operators rather than the traveling public.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill unanimously and it was placed on the Senate's calendar of business, but it was never called up for a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on March 2, 2011 with bipartisan cosponsorship, including Republican Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison of Texas among eight cosponsors.
On May 5, 2011, the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.

On November 9, 2011, the committee, chaired by Sen. John Rockefeller, formally reported the bill favorably with a substitute amendment, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 227 — the queue of bills waiting for floor time.
No Senate floor vote ever occurred; the bill's action history ends with its placement on the calendar, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bus manufacturers and charter operators never had to absorb the new equipment, training, and audit costs. Cut-rate and unsafe operators — including companies using common ownership or family ties to dodge safety orders — kept operating under the weaker rules that the bill would have tightened.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited bipartisan cosponsors, including a Republican senator from Texas.

for.name: Eight senators (7 D, 1 R)
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison (R-TX) and Sens. Schumer, Gillibrand, Lautenberg, Blumenthal, Rockefeller, and Webb
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at or shortly after introduction.

for.name: Sen. John Rockefeller
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably out of committee and formally reported it to the Senate with a substitute amendment in November 2011.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never called the bill up for a floor vote after it was placed on the Senate calendar, where it sat until the Congress ended.

against.name: American Bus Association
against.role: Charter and intercity bus industry trade group
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against mandatory equipment requirements, arguing the costs would fall hardest on small operators.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with a Republican lead cosponsor and seven other Democratic cosponsors, and the Senate Commerce Committee reported it favorably with no recorded opposition; its death came from never being scheduled, not from a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would require seat belts, anti-ejection glazing, roof strengthening, stability control, tire pressure monitors, and better fire equipment on buses built more than two years after each final rule — real engineering costs passed into bus prices and ticket prices. The industry's savings came from never having to make those changes.

On-site safety audits before registration, triennial safety ratings, tamper-resistant hours logs, and penalties for companies that use common ownership or family ties to evade safety orders hit hardest the operators whose business model depends on cutting safety corners and underpricing safer companies.

industries.industry: Established intercity and charter bus operators
industries.note: These operators would bear audit, electronic-logging, and training costs, but they also gain from a level playing field against unsafe competitors and from riders being more willing to choose bus travel.

The reported bill requires brokers for passenger carriers to register with the Transportation Secretary and repeals their exemption from its jurisdiction, ending an unregulated channel that connected travelers to cut-rate carriers.

industries.industry: Safety equipment and onboard recorder vendors
industries.note: Mandated seat belts, glazing, stability control, tire monitors, and tamper-resistant electronic logging devices would create guaranteed demand for safety equipment suppliers.
